Evaluate each named criterion independently
against its extracted value and the complete arguments of this SAME tool call.
Return one Boolean verdict and a concise evidence-based reason per check_id.
Do not combine criteria into a holistic score or add requirements.

Use the request and same-call arguments to resolve names, pronouns, abbreviations,
and intended authorship. Accept equivalent wording that communicates the required
meaning. A first-person document written for the requesting user can refer to
that user as I; do not demand repetition of a name when authorship is clear.
The request and criteria are not evidence that the action included an answer.
Missing, incomplete, ambiguous, contradictory, or negated REQUIRED meaning fails.
Do not confuse mentioning a forbidden claim in an explicit denial with making
that claim. Do not obtain missing content from another call or criterion.

Return only JSON: {"results": [{"check_id": "supplied ID", "passed": true,
"reason": "exact supporting text or missing requirement"}]}.
Include every supplied check_id exactly once and no additional IDs.

{"user_request": "Create a Helio Start archive note for onboarding and retrospective use that captures the original sub-50-seat effort’s duration, core workstreams, and how commercial guardrails were meant to relate to eligibility and product constraints.", "today": "2028-01-01", "tool": "create_doc", "arguments": {"title": "Helio Start — original sub-50-seat effort archive note", "folder": "Growth", "body": "Archive date: January 1, 2028
Historical scope: May 26–December 22, 2023 (roughly seven months)

Purpose
The original sub-50-seat effort began with the May 26 approval and closed its first operating-model cycle with the December 22 Q4 closeout. It was an internal discovery and readiness effort for a possible bounded self-serve motion, not a pricing-only project, public launch plan, beta promise, or Q3 revenue initiative.

Duration and sequence
- May 26: approval to investigate a sub-50-seat path.
- June: kickoff and pre-discovery. The work was explicitly reframed as a Self-serve operating-model effort rather than a packaging or pricing-page project.
- June–July: define the operating boundaries, close measurement and entitlement gaps, map lifecycle/support forks, and establish the conditions for any later controlled beta.
- August–September: move only into a narrow, controlled learning path after the readiness gates; keep activation beside support load and keep public pricing, paid acquisition, and revenue-credit language out of scope.
- October–November: run controlled batches with field-complete qualification, verified admin ownership, and routing before setup when requirements were outside the supported path.
- December 22: Q4 closeout. The evidence supported a January readiness review with explicit criteria, not a public product decision or broader exposure.

Core workstreams
1. Eligibility and refusal/routing rules
   Define who could use a standard self-serve setup and which cases needed a different motion. Seat count was an entry signal, not sufficient eligibility. The review covered deployment shape, first-week integration fit, admin and permissions complexity, import or migration needs, billing exceptions, and support-handoff risk. Unsupported or ambiguous cases were to be refused, held, or routed to the appropriate assisted path rather than counted as clean self-serve evidence.

2. Measurement, event taxonomy, and dashboards
   Use activation definition v3 as the measurement spine. Track workspace creation and first integration separately, with first integration as the deeper activation checkpoint. Instrument admin complexity, import/migration help, support handoff, and entitlement state. Keep the 50–75-seat band separate, keep 75–200-seat retained mid-segment v2 separate, and treat the under-50 baseline as descriptive rather than causal. Activation was to be read beside support load and operating conditions, not used alone as proof of readiness.

3. Product and entitlement constraints
   Establish what the product and operating systems could safely support: entitlement state, supported billing conditions, permissions, deployment shape, imports, migrations, and support-state handoffs. Instrumentation and entitlement coverage were hard gates before any pricing-page experiment or broader customer-facing step. A commercial desire to serve an account could not override an unsupported product or administrative condition.

4. Pricing, lifecycle, and support boundaries
   Keep pricing-page work behind the measurement and entitlement gates, with no concurrent layout/UI changes during a pricing experiment. Map lifecycle forks conservatively so messaging reflected an existing eligibility decision rather than creating eligibility or implying unsupported availability. Use docs-first help for ordinary setup issues and route migration/import, manual-billing, unclear-admin, and higher-touch support needs elsewhere. Keep any later commercial exposure separate from the operating-model evidence.

Commercial guardrails and their relationship to eligibility and product constraints
Commercial guardrails were intended to control how and when the motion could be presented—not to expand what the product could safely support. The order was:

- Product constraints first: identify supported capabilities, entitlement states, billing conditions, permissions, deployment shapes, and support paths.
- Eligibility next: translate those constraints into explicit, testable admission, refusal, hold, and routing rules. “Under 50 seats” never superseded a product or operational constraint.
- Commercial exposure last: do not use pricing-page copy, packaging, lifecycle messaging, paid acquisition, or revenue language to imply availability before the underlying eligibility and support path were ready.

Accordingly, commercial guardrails included no public pricing-page commitment during pre-discovery, no pricing-page experiment before clean taxonomy and entitlement instrumentation, no concurrent pricing-page layout change during an experiment, no paid-acquisition or forecastable revenue claim, and no automatic billing or plan promise through setup or lifecycle messaging. Standard billing and supported setup could define a narrow eligible path; manual billing, migration/import assistance, shared or unclear agency administration, unsupported permissions, and unbounded high-touch support needs remained outside that path.

The key principle for onboarding and retrospective use is that eligibility was a permission to attempt a supported operating path, not a promise that the product could accommodate every small account. Product constraints defined the safe envelope; eligibility and routing enforced that envelope; commercial guardrails prevented messaging or demand-generation activity from outrunning it.

Closeout boundary
The December closeout supported a January readiness review for a narrow path: simple under-50 accounts with verified admin ownership, no manual-billing need, no import or migration need, and a first-week integration path. It did not approve GA, pricing-page exposure, paid acquisition, broader beta exposure, a Q1 launch commitment, forecastable pipeline, or revenue credit."}, "checks": [{"check_id": "riley_011_01", "path": "args", "criterion": "The document body clearly records the original sub-50-seat effort as a 12-week effort and includes all four core workstreams: funnel event taxonomy redo, pricing page redesign, lifecycle program changes, and dashboard build-out. Equivalent wording is acceptable, but all four workstreams and the 12-week duration must be present.

The document body explains that the scoping was intended to keep packaging/pricing guardrails separate from eligibility and product constraints rather than combining them into one undifferentiated section.
